heading: The pilgrimage state
body: Uttarakhand's history is largely a history of altitude: a Himalayan borderland whose ruling dynasties, unlike those of the plains, were shaped as much by the mountains' geography as by conquest. The earliest recorded power in the region belonged to the Kunindas, from around the 2nd century BCE, who practised an early form of Shaivism and traded salt across the passes into western Tibet. Over the following centuries the region split into two broad zones that still structure it today — Kumaon, where the Katyuri and later Chand dynasties held power roughly from the 8th to the 18th centuries, and Garhwal, unified from fifty-two smaller principalities into a single kingdom in the 14th century by King Ajay Pal of the Parmar dynasty, whose line ruled until 1803.

Both kingdoms fell to the same outside power within a few years of each other: the expanding Gurkha Empire of Nepal took Kumaon's capital, Almora, in 1791, and the Garhwal kingdom in 1804. Gurkha rule did not last — the Anglo-Nepalese War ended in 1816 with the Treaty of Sugauli, under which the British restored a western remnant of the Garhwal kingdom at Tehri while annexing the rest of Garhwal and all of Kumaon directly.

Running underneath this political history is a much older religious one that gives the region its modern identity: the Char Dham, four Himalayan pilgrimage sites — Kedarnath, Badrinath, Gangotri and Yamunotri — that draw hundreds of thousands of pilgrims each year and that tradition credits the 9th-century philosopher Adi Shankaracharya with renovating and re-establishing as a pilgrimage circuit. Long before Uttarakhand existed as an administrative unit, it existed in the religious imagination as the source of the Ganga and Yamuna and the gateway to Mount Kailash, and that older identity has outlasted every dynasty that ruled the land beneath it.
The sites on this map draw on both threads — the Kumaon and Garhwal courts that governed the hills, and the pilgrimage geography that gave them their lasting significance.
